title: What Is Knitting Frame? — Definition
body:
Cloth-making before synthetics and automation: the spinning wheel and hand loom, the spinning jenny/mule/frame, the power loom and Jacquard, fulling mills, and the natural fibers — wool, flax, cotton, silk — with their dyes, weaves, and finishing.

In the context of this database, the Knitting Frame is presented as one textile record among the textile history family. 1589's stocking: the 1589 — the 1589's.

title: Origins and History of Knitting Frame
body:
The Knitting Frame belongs to the 1589–1800s era and traces to William Lee.

Spinning and weaving are Neolithic; the spinning wheel reached Europe by the 1200s and India made the world's finest muslins. The 18th century mechanized it: flying shuttle (1733), spinning jenny (1764), water frame (1769), mule (1779), power loom (1785), Jacquard cards (1804), the sewing machine (1846/1851) — Lancashire's mills and Lowell's girls industrialized cloth. Natural dyes (madder, woad, indigo, cochineal) gave way to Perkin's mauveine (1856) — the first aniline dye. The cotton gin (1793) scaled fiber; the woolen fulling mill finished cloth for centuries.

Within that longer story, Knitting Frame: The 1589; the 1600s'. The Lee is the knit’s frame.

title: How Knitting Frame Works
body:
Spinning drafts fibers and twists them into yarn (the wheel's ratio sets twist); weaving interlaces warp (lengthwise) and weft (crosswise) in plain, twill, or satin structures. The Jacquard head lifts warp threads per punched card for figured patterns. Fulling shrinks and felts woolen cloth; dyeing fixes color with mordants. The sewing machine's lockstitch (needle + shuttle/bobbin) mechanized seaming.

Applied to the Knitting Frame (1589–1800s, William Lee): The Lee is the knit’s frame.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Knitting Frame — Components
body:
Every Knitting Frame is an assembly of the textile history family's standard parts:

• Spinning wheel — Drive wheel, spindle/flyer, treadle; twist and draft.
• Loom & harness — Warp control; treadles lift shafts.
• Jacquard head — Card-selected patterning.
• Shuttle & reed — Weft insertion and beat-up.
• Cards & lacing — Punched pattern programs.
• Fulling stocks — Pounding mills felting wool.
• Dye vats & mordants — Color chemistry of the natural palette.
• Sewing machine head — Needle bar, shuttle, feed dogs.
• Gin & picker — Fiber cleaning machines.
• Niddy-noddy / swift — Yarn measuring and handling.

When examining a surviving Knitting Frame, identify these parts in order: Spinning wheel, Loom & harness, Jacquard head, Shuttle & reed, Cards & lacing, Fulling stocks.

title: Textile History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of textile history:

• warp / weft — Lengthwise / crosswise threads.
• plain / twill / satin — The three fundamental weaves.
• pick — One weft pass; picks per inch = density.
• sley / reed — Beating the weft into place.
• fulling — Shrinking/felting woolen cloth.
• mordant — Fixative bonding dye to fiber.
• aniline dyes — Perkin 1856; coal-tar color revolution.
• shuttle — Weft carrier; flying shuttle mechanized it.
• bobbin / shuttle (sewing) — Lockstitch's lower thread.
• feed dogs — Sewing machine's fabric movers.

title: Knitting Frame in Culture
body:
Cloth is civilization's first industry: 'spinsters', 'web' (the loom's), 'Luddite' (the stocking-frame wreckers of 1811). Paisley, denim, tartan — patterns as identity. The sewing circle, the quilting bee, the mill girl's twelve-hour day — textiles wove social history. Indigo and madder dyed empires' uniforms.

The Knitting Frame carries that cultural charge directly: The Lee is the knit’s frame.

title: Collecting and Preserving Knitting Frame
body:
Spinning wheels: check for complete flyers and drive bands. Looms need space; table looms are the entry. Sewing machines (Singer 27/66/201) are plentiful — the 201 is the machinist's choice. Shuttle collections and textile tools are affordable folk art.

For the Knitting Frame specifically: 1589's stocking: the 1589 — the 1589's.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working Knitting Frame with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: Knitting Frame Restoration Guide
body:
Wood: clean, oil, repair joinery. Leather drive bands: replace and dress. Sewing machines: clean lint, oil per diagram, time the hook. Looms: check reeds and heddles; replace worn parts.

Restoration order for a Knitting Frame: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical textile record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Knitting Frame — Weave draft + thread calculator (Runnable Python)
body:
Generates a plain/twill weave draft from a threading draft and computes yarn needs — the loom's programming, on paper first.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Knitting Frame so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Weave draft generator: threading x treadling -> drawdown (public-domain logic)
def drawdown(threading, treadling, tieup):
    # threading: list of shaft per warp end; treadling: shaft combo per pick
    rows = []
    for combo in treadling:
        lifted = set()
        for s in combo:
            lifted.update(tieup[s])
        rows.append(["X" if (i in lifted) == (threading[i] in combo) else "."
                     for i in range(len(threading))])
    return rows

threading = [1,2,3,4]*8          # straight draw on 4 shafts
tieup = {1:[1,2], 2:[2,3], 3:[3,4], 4:[4,1]}  # 2/2 twill
treadling = [[1],[2],[3],[4]]*2
dd = drawdown(threading, treadling, tieup)
print("2/2 twill drawdown (X = warp up):")
for r in dd[:8]:
    print("".join(r[:16]))

# Yarn estimate: warp ends x length / 840 (cotton count) etc. (simplified)
ends, length_yd = 320, 6
print(f"\nwarp yarn: {ends} ends x {length_yd} yd = {ends*length_yd} yd")
